entry: City in Sudan, the second most populous in the country, on the west bank of the [[Nile|River Nile]] opposite [[Khartoum]]. It is an important road hub. After the siege of Khartoum, the city grew rapidly following the building of the tomb of the Mahdi, who died of [[Typhus|typhus]]. In the Battle of Omdurman in 1898, British forces under Horatio Herbert Kitchener defeated the Mahdist army, killing at least 10,000 Sudanese while losing 48 soldiers. Kitchener then ordered the Mahdi's tomb desecrated, and [[Winston Churchill]] wrote that he "carried off the Mahdi's head in a kerosene can as a trophy." Most of the city was destroyed in the battle, but the tomb was later restored. During the [[Sudanese civil war (2023–present)|Sudanese civil war]], the Rapid Support Forces occupied the city from April 2023 to May 2025.

Globular cluster in the constellation [[Centaurus]], 17,090 light-years (5,240 parsecs) from [[Earth]]. It was first identified as a non-stellar object by [[Edmond Halley]] in 1677, having been catalogued by [[Ptolemy]] around 150 AD as a star. It is the largest known globular cluster in the [[Milky Way]], about 150 light-years across, with an estimated 10 million stars and a total mass of 4 million [[Solar mass|solar masses]]. Unlike most globular clusters, it is thought to be the core remnant of a disrupted [[Dwarf galaxy|dwarf galaxy]]. A 2008 study using the [[Hubble Space Telescope]] and the Gemini Observatory found evidence of an intermediate-mass black hole at its center, although this is disputed. It is one of the few globular clusters visible to the naked eye.

City (pop., 2024: 1,104,485) in southwestern [[Siberia]], Russia, and administrative center of Omsk Oblast. It is the third largest city in Siberia after [[Novosibirsk]] and Krasnoyarsk, and the twelfth-largest in Russia. The fortress founded in 1716 at the confluence of the Om and Irtysh rivers was built to secure the trade route to [[China]]. Omsk is a transport node on the [[Trans-Siberian Railway]]. In the Soviet era it became an industrial center focused on oil refining, petrochemicals and heavy engineering. During the [[Russian Civil War]] it briefly served as the capital of the anti-Bolshevik Russian State and held the imperial gold reserves. The city is the seat of the bishop of Omsk and Tara.

Philosophical work in prose and verse by the Roman philosopher Boethius. Written in 523 while Boethius awaited execution for treason under the Ostrogothic king [[Theodoric the Great|Theodoric]], it is often described as the last great Western work of the Classical Period. It takes the form of a dialogue between Boethius and a personification of philosophy, "Lady Philosophy," who argues that wealth, fame and power are fleeting and that true happiness lies in [[Virtue|virtue]] and things of the mind. The work treats the problem of evil, [[Free will|free will]] and [[Predestination|predestination]], human nature and justice. It heavily influenced [[Late antiquity|late antiquity]] and [[Middle Ages|medieval]] Christianity, and [[Alfred the Great]] translated it into [[Old English]].

Scientific work by the English naturalist [[Charles Darwin]], published November 24, 1859. Considered the foundation of evolutionary biology, it argued that populations evolve over generations through [[Natural selection|natural selection]] and that the diversity of life arose by [[Evolution|common descent]] through a branching pattern. Darwin drew on evidence collected on the Beagle expedition in the 1830s and on later research, correspondence and experiments. Written for non-specialist readers, it sparked widespread debate over its implications for the fixity of [[Species|species]] and for religion, at a time when the English scientific establishment was closely tied to the [[Church of England]]. Within two decades most scientists accepted that evolution had occurred, although natural selection was slow to gain prominence. After the modern evolutionary synthesis of the 1930s and 1940s, natural selection became the unifying concept of the life sciences.

1954 American crime drama film directed by [[Elia Kazan]]. Written by Budd Schulberg, it stars [[Marlon Brando]] as a former boxer who testifies against a corrupt union boss on the Hoboken waterfront. It was inspired by Malcolm Johnson's Pulitzer Prize-winning newspaper articles on longshoremen's union corruption. The film features [[Eva Marie Saint]] in her film debut, and its score by [[Leonard Bernstein]] is his only original film score. It received twelve [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations and won eight, including Best Picture. In 1989 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for preservation in the National Film Registry.

Branch of medicine dealing with the study, diagnosis, treatment and prevention of [[Cancer|cancer]]. Practitioners are called oncologists, a term derived from the Greek *onkos*, meaning tumor, which the Greek physician Galen first used to describe tumors. Cancer was first documented in humans in Egypt around 3000 BC, when the Edwin Smith papyrus described a form of cancer as "a bulging tumor of the breast." Oncology covers diagnosis, therapy, monitoring after treatment, palliative care, screening and clinical research into cancer treatments. Diagnosis relies on a [[Biopsy|biopsy]] examined by a pathologist, with [[Endoscopy]] and [[Medical imaging|imaging]] such as X-rays, CT scanning, MRI and ultrasound used to locate suspicious tissue. Treatment may combine [[Surgery|surgery]], [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]] and [[Radiation therapy|radiation therapy]], depending on the cancer, and surgery is attempted when a tumor can be removed entirely. Oncologists often specialize by organ or modality, such as breast, brain or radiation oncology.

English–Irish pop boy band (2010–2016). Formed in London in 2010 on the British show The X Factor, the group comprised Niall Horan, Liam Payne, Harry Styles, Louis Tomlinson and Zayn Malik (until 2015). Propelled to success by [[Social media|social media]], it sold over 70 million records. Its debut album *Up All Night* (2011) was the first by a British act to top the Billboard 200, and its first four albums debuted at number one. Its 2014 Where We Are Tour grossed $290 million, the highest for a vocal group. It won nearly 200 awards before an indefinite hiatus in 2016.

headword: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest
sort_key: one flew over the cuckoos nest
entry: 1975 American psychological comedy-drama film directed by Miloš Forman, based on the 1962 novel by [[Ken Kesey]]. [[Jack Nicholson]] plays Randle McMurphy, who feigns mental illness to avoid hard labor and is placed on a ward ruled by Nurse Ratched, played by Louise Fletcher. Filmed at the Oregon State Hospital, an actual [[Psychiatric hospital|psychiatric hospital]] in [[Oregon]], it won all five major [[Academy Awards]], becoming the second of three films to do so, after *It Happened One Night* (1934) and before *The Silence of the Lambs* (1991). In 1993 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry.

1967 [[Novel|novel]] by Colombian author [[Gabriel García Márquez]]. It traces seven generations of the Buendía family in the fictional town of Macondo, and its magical realist style made it a representative work of the [[Latin America|Latin American]] Boom of the 1960s and 1970s. Often cited as one of the supreme achievements in world literature, it was recognized at the 4th International Conference of the Spanish Language in 2007 as one of the most important works in the [[Spanish language]]. First published in May 1967 by Editorial Sudamericana in [[Buenos Aires]], it has been translated into 46 languages and sold more than 50 million copies. An authorized 16-episode TV series, executive produced by García Márquez's sons, ran on [[Netflix]].

Japanese [[Manga|manga]] series by Eiichiro Oda. Serialized in Shueisha's [[Weekly Shōnen Jump]] since July 1997, it follows the pirate [[Monkey D. Luffy]] and his crew, the Straw Hats, in a search for the treasure known as the One Piece, which would make him King of the Pirates. Its chapters were compiled in 115 volumes as of July 2026, and it had over 600 million copies in circulation by March 2026, making it the best-selling manga series ever. It set Guinness World Records in 2015 and 2022 for most copies published for the same comic book series by a single author. Toei Animation's [[Anime|anime]] adaptation premiered in 1999, and a live-action [[Netflix]] series followed in 2023. The manga was licensed for English-language release in North America and the [[United Kingdom]] by Viz Media.

Collection of Middle Eastern folk tales, compiled in [[Arabic]] during the [[Islamic Golden Age]] and known in English as *The Arabian Nights*. Its frame story concerns King Shahryar, who vowed to execute each new bride after his first wife's betrayal; the vizier's daughter Scheherazade volunteers to marry him and tells him tales each night, leaving each unfinished at dawn to postpone her death. The collection was assembled over many centuries across [[West Asia]], Central Asia, South Asia and North Africa, and it has no canonical text or order. [[Aladdin]] and the Wonderful Lamp and [[Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves]] were not in the original Arabic but were added by the French translator Antoine Galland, who heard them from the [[Syria|Syrian]] writer Hanna Diyab in [[Paris]] in 1709. The tales feature [[Jinn|jinn]], merchants and caliphs.

Population control policy in [[China]], in force from 1979 to 2015. A near-universal one-child limit was imposed in 1980 and written into the constitution in 1982. Exceptions included rural families whose first child was a daughter and some ethnic minorities; by 1984 only about 35.4% of the population was subject to the original restriction. Families who violated the limit faced large fines, and enforcement sometimes included forced [[Abortion|abortion]] and [[Sterilization (medicine)|sterilization]]. The policy skewed the sex ratio toward men and contributed to the abandonment of infant girls, creating what critics call a generation of "missing women." The limit was raised to two children in 2015 and to three in 2021, and all limits were removed in July 2021. The [[Chinese Communist Party]] credits the policy with preventing 400 million births, a figure some scholars dispute, while the policy has been widely criticized in the West for [[Human rights|human rights]] violations.

[[Vegetable|Bulbous vegetable]] (*Allium cepa*), the most widely cultivated species of the [[Genus|genus]] *Allium*. It is a biennial usually grown as an annual, with hollow, bluish-green leaves and a bulb formed from shortened underground stems and fleshy scale leaves. The shallot, classed as a separate species until 2011, is a botanical variety of the onion. Close relatives include [[Garlic]], scallion, [[Leek]] and chives. The onion is known only from cultivation, though related wild species occur in [[Central Asia]] and [[Iran]]. Onions were placed in [[Ancient Egypt]] tombs as symbols of eternity, and they are now produced on every continent except Antarctica. Raw onions are about 89% water and contain 9.3 g of carbohydrates per 100 g. They can be eaten raw, cooked, pickled or dried, and when chopped they release chemicals that can irritate the eyes. The species was first formally described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753.

British television [[Sitcom|sitcom]] (1981–2003). Created and written by John Sullivan, it follows the get-rich-quick schemes of market trader Derek "Del Boy" Trotter, played by David Jason, and his younger half-brother Rodney, played by Nicholas Lyndhurst, in working-class Peckham, London. Seven series and sixteen Christmas specials aired on BBC One from 1981 to 1996. The 1996 episode "Time on Our Hands" drew 24.3 million viewers, the largest UK audience for a sitcom episode. The series added several phrases to English and was voted Britain's Best Sitcom in a 2004 BBC poll. A spin-off, *The Green Green Grass*, followed.

Type of word, or the process of forming one, that imitates the sound it describes. Common English examples include *oink*, *meow*, *roar* and *hiccup*. Such words follow each language's phonetic rules, so a clock says *tick tock* in English, *tic tac* in Spanish and Italian, and *kachi kachi* in Japanese, and *ṭik-ṭik* in [[Hindi]] and [[Urdu]]. A frog's croak varies by species: in [[Ancient Greek]], [[Aristophanes]] wrote *brekekekex koax koax* in *The Frogs*, while English has *ribbit* for North American frogs and *croak* for the common frog. The bird name [[Cuckoo]] has kept its pronunciation for centuries.

Southernmost and most populous province of [[Canada]]. Over 14 million people, about 38.5% of the national population according to the 2021 census, live there. Ontario is the second-largest province by area after [[Quebec]]. Its capital is [[Toronto]], the country's most populous city, and the national capital, [[Ottawa]], is also in the province. Ontario borders [[Manitoba]] to the west and Hudson Bay and James Bay to the north. Its southern border with the United States, a 2,700-kilometre (1,700 mi) line, follows rivers and lakes of the [[Great Lakes]] for nearly its full length. Most of the population and arable land lie in Southern Ontario, where manufacturing is central to the economy, while the sparsely populated north, covered largely by the [[Canadian Shield]], depends on mining and forestry. The name is thought to be of Indigenous origin, and the province was established at Confederation in 1867.

Origination and development of an organism, usually from fertilization of the egg to [[Adult|adulthood]]. It includes physical and psychological development, such as moral development, and covers morphogenesis, tissue growth and the differentiation of cells. Ontogeny is studied in [[Developmental biology|developmental biology]], [[Embryo|embryology]], [[Genetics]], [[Cell biology]] and [[Developmental psychology]]. It is distinct from phylogeny, the evolutionary history of a species, although developmental processes can influence [[Evolution|evolution]]. The term was coined in the 1860s by the German zoologist [[Ernst Haeckel]], who proposed that ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny; the marine biologist Walter Garstang later reversed this relationship, arguing that ontogeny creates phylogeny. Anthropologists also use the term.

In information science, a formal specification of the concepts, properties and relations within a domain. Ontologies define classes, attributes and relationships, often with logical axioms, so that databases and software agents can share knowledge without ambiguity. The approach grew out of [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] research in the 1980s and was formalized in [[Computer science]] during the 1990s, when Tom Gruber defined an ontology as an "explicit specification of a conceptualization" in 1993. Editors such as Protégé are used in biomedical informatics and industry. Ontology is also a branch of [[Philosophy]], intersecting [[Metaphysics]] and [[Epistemology]], concerned with the nature of reality.

Typically black-and-white banded variety of [[Agate|agate]]. Its bands are parallel, unlike the chaotic banding of most agates, and it is formed of chalcedony, a microcrystalline form of [[Quartz|quartz]]. Sardonyx has red to brown bands alternating with black or white. The name derives from the [[Ancient Greek]] *onyx*, meaning claw or fingernail. Much of the carved "onyx" sold today is banded [[Calcite]], and most "black onyx" is artificially dyed; [[Pliny the Elder]] described such treatments in Roman times. Onyx has long been used for carving cameos and jewelry, with major occurrences in Brazil, India, Madagascar, Mexico and the United States.

Fungus-like eukaryotic microorganism in the [[Stramenopile|stramenopiles]] lineage, distinct from true fungi. Filamentous and heterotrophic, oomycetes reproduce sexually, forming overwintering oospores, and asexually, forming motile zoospores. Many are [[Pathogen|pathogens]] of plants, including the causes of late blight of [[Potato|potato]] and sudden oak death, while others are saprophytes. They are called water molds because of their preference for moist habitats, though most species are terrestrial. Oomycetes were once grouped with [[Fungus|fungi]] because of their similar appearance, but molecular studies placed them with the stramenopiles, which include some [[Algae|algae]] and [[Diatom|diatoms]]. The earliest fossil records date to the [[Devonian]], about 407 million years ago.

Hypothesized cloud of icy planetesimals surrounding the [[Sun]] at distances of 2,000 to 200,000 [[Astronomical unit|AU]]. Dutch astronomer Jan Oort proposed it in 1950 to explain the replenishment of long-period [[Comet|comets]] entering the inner Solar System. The cloud is thought to have an inner disc aligned with the [[Ecliptic]] and a spherical outer shell; its innermost part lies more than a thousand times as far from the Sun as the [[Kuiper belt]]. Astronomers hypothesize that its material formed near the Sun and was scattered outward by the [[Giant planet|giant planets]]. The outer cloud is only loosely bound to the Sun and is perturbed by passing stars and the [[Milky Way]], which occasionally send comets inward. Direct observation is not possible with present imaging technology.

Hydrated amorphous form of silica (SiO₂·nH₂O), classified as a [[Mineral|mineraloid]]. Its water content ranges from 3% to 21% by mass, usually 6% to 10%. Precious opal shows play-of-color, caused by ordered silica spheres of 150–300 nm that diffract light; common opal lacks this effect. Black opal is the rarest, while white, gray and green opals are the most common. Opal forms at low temperatures in fissures of rocks such as [[Sandstone]] and [[Basalt]]. Its name is believed to derive from the Sanskrit *upala*, meaning jewel. Australia produces over 95% of the world's precious opal.

Basic subset of a [[Topological space|topological space]], generalizing an open interval of the [[Real number|real line]]. In a [[Metric space|metric space]], a set is open if every point in it has a surrounding ball of nearby points that also lie in the set. More generally, a [[Topology|topology]] is a collection of subsets that contains the empty set and the whole space and is closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections; its members are the open sets. Open sets allow continuity, connectedness and compactness to be defined without a distance. A [[Manifold|manifold]] resembles an open set of [[Euclidean space]] near each point, yet no distance is defined on it in general. The discrete topology makes every subset open, while the indiscrete topology allows only the empty set and the whole space.

Practice of publishing digital resources alongside their source files, enabling use, study, modification and redistribution. Historically associated with [[Open-source software]], the concept has been applied to open hardware, open educational resources and open fonts. Such resources are made available under open licenses or [[Public domain|public-domain]] dedications, which grant reuse rights while the author keeps ownership under [[Copyright]]. Licenses vary by field: the SIL Open Font License prohibits standalone sale of font files, the CERN Open Hardware Licence covers patent rights, and the Open Database License addresses database rights. Access to source files is needed to modify a resource, yet a 2016 study of Thingiverse found that 84% of shared designs were in STL format, a distribution format. The term also denotes publicly available sources of information, as in open-source intelligence (OSINT).
